## Synthesis Overview

PR #347 delivers three focused changes: recap persistence is moved unconditionally outside the `events` guard in the orchestrator (the core bug fix for issue #346); empty character/setting context blocks are suppressed in the direct-path prompt to avoid empty XML noise; and documentation is corrected to reflect per-chapter wiki updates. All three reviewers agree the orchestrator refactor itself is correct. The primary area of concern — reported unanimously — is that the `write_chapter_direct.md` variable rename (`character_context` / `setting_context` → `character_context_block` / `setting_context_block`) was not propagated to the integration smoke test or the feature documentation, leaving the test sending malformed prompts to the LLM and the docs describing a contract that no longer exists. Two majority findings flag an empty-list repr regression in recap persistence and stale `sheet-evolution` references in the granular-checkpointing doc.

**Model Agreement Score:** 8/10 — strong agreement on the two highest-priority findings; minor divergence on severity rating and the scope of the events fix.

## Consensus Findings

### ★★★ Unanimous Findings (All Three Models Agree)

---

```
[U-C-01] test_prompt_verification.py not updated for variable rename
Severity: Critical
Category: Testing / Correctness
File: tests/integration/test_prompt_verification.py
Lines: 152–153
Detail: The PR renames the template variables in prompts/chapters/write_chapter_direct.md from
        `character_context` / `setting_context` to `character_context_block` / `setting_context_block`.
        The production caller (ChapterWriterAgent) was updated. However,
        TestPromptVerification::test_chapters_write_chapter_direct still passes the old keys
        `character_context` and `setting_context`. Because PromptLoader._substitute_variables
        performs best-effort string replacement and does not raise on unresolved keys, the rendered
        prompt retains the literal tokens `{character_context_block}` and `{setting_context_block}`.
        The test then sends this malformed prompt to the live LLM provider and only checks the model
        output for tool-calling narration — it does not detect the unresolved placeholders. Verified
        on disk: lines 152–153 still use old key names.
Models: Claude ✓  GPT ✓  Gemini ✓
Severity note: Claude and Gemini rate Critical; GPT rates Warning. Critical is correct — the test
               is actively sending structurally broken prompts to the model on every CI run.
Suggestion: Update the variables dict to pass `"character_context_block": ""` and
            `"setting_context_block": ""`. Optionally add a pre-submission assertion that the
            rendered prompt contains no unresolved `{...}` tokens.
```

### ★★☆ Majority Findings (Two of Three Models Agree)

---

```
[M-W-01] Events repr regression — `str([])` writes `"[]"` to recap_events.md; mocks use wrong type
Severity: Warning
Category: Correctness / Testing
File (production): src/presentation/orchestrator.py (line 1832)
File (test): tests/unit/test_orchestrator.py (lines 2031, 2134, 2199, 2332, 2483)
Detail: Moving recap persistence unconditionally outside the events guard introduced a subtle
        regression. The persistence dict comprehension at line 1832 calls
        `str(recap_result.get(field, ""))`. When events is an empty Python list `[]`,
        `str([])` yields the repr string `"[]"`, which is written to recap_events.md.
        In production, RecapWriterAgent.run() never returns `[]` — on failure it returns
        `{"events": "", ...}` (strings throughout). However, multiple test mocks across the file
        (lines 2031, 2134, 2199, 2332, 2483) return `{"events": []}`, making `[]` the defacto test
        value. The mocks therefore do not reflect the real return type and the new
        test_recap_persisted_when_events_empty does not catch whether the orchestrator would write
        an empty string vs `"[]"` to disk. Verified: line 1832 in orchestrator.py confirmed;
        test mock pattern confirmed at all five locations.
Models: Claude ✓  GPT ✗  Gemini ✓
Dissenting view: GPT did not raise this finding. Given that the real agent never returns `[]`,
                 GPT may have assessed the production regression risk as negligible. The mock
                 type mismatch remains a real defect regardless.
Suggestion (two-part):
  1. Production defense: change `str(recap_result.get(field, ""))` to
     `str(recap_result.get(field) or "")` so falsy non-string values (empty list, None) write
     an empty file rather than their repr.
  2. Test fix: change all `{"events": []}` mocks to `{"events": ""}` to match the real
     RecapWriterAgent.run() return type.
```

```
[M-S-01] Empty `## CHARACTER & SETTING CONTEXT` heading when both context blocks are absent
Severity: Suggestion
Category: Style
File: prompts/chapters/write_chapter_direct.md
Lines: 27–33 (approx.)
Detail: When both `character_context_block` and `setting_context_block` resolve to empty strings
        (e.g., when the wiki snapshot path is active), the rendered prompt contains the heading
        `## CHARACTER & SETTING CONTEXT` followed immediately by blank lines and then `## YOUR TASK`.
        The old behaviour produced empty XML tags; this PR replaces that with an empty heading.
        Neither is harmful to correctness — the LLM proceeds normally — but an empty heading
        signals expected content was omitted rather than deliberately absent.
Models: Claude ✓  GPT ✗  Gemini ✓
Dissenting view: GPT did not surface this. It is a minor cosmetic issue and reasonable to defer.
Suggestion: Consider guarding the entire section (heading + blocks) with a conditional so it is
            suppressed entirely when both blocks are empty, or accept the current state as a
            tolerable improvement over empty XML tags.
```

Severity: Suggestion

Detail: The new test correctly exercises the core fix (recap persisted when events is falsy) and

            addressing together in the same fix pass to prevent a silent regression in future.

## Divergence Analysis

```
[D-01] Severity of U-C-01 (test_prompt_verification.py stale variable names)
Claude says:  Critical — malformed prompts sent to LLM on every test run
GPT says:     Warning — regression in the prompt contract, but test still passes superficially
Gemini says:  Critical — integration test verifies LLM response against a broken prompt template
Assessment:   Claude and Gemini (2/3) are correct. The rendered prompt contains literal
              `{character_context_block}` tokens when the test runs against a live provider.
              The fact that the `_assert_no_tool_calling` check passes does not make the test
              valid — it is testing LLM behaviour on a structurally malformed input. Critical
              is the appropriate severity. GPT's Warning rating is the outlier.
Resolution:   Retained as Critical in [U-C-01].
```

```
[D-02] Root cause framing for the events regression (M-W-01)
Claude says:  Production code defect — `str([])` writes `"[]"`; fix with `or ""` guard in orchestrator
GPT says:     Not raised
Gemini says:  Mock defect — mocks return `[]` which doesn't match real return type (string)
Assessment:   Both Claude and Gemini are correct, and the two aspects are complementary rather
              than contradictory. The real RecapWriterAgent never returns `[]` (confirmed by reading
              recap_writer.py: failure path returns `{"events": ""}`, success path returns a string).
              So the production regression is theoretical; the mock type mismatch is practical.
              Claude's suggested `or ""` guard is sound defensive programming. Gemini's mock fix
              is required to make the test reflect real agent behaviour.
Resolution:   Captured both aspects in [M-W-01] as a two-part fix.
```

```
[D-03] Scope of stale sheet-evolution references
Claude says:  granular-checkpointing.md only (lines 99, 172, 189)
GPT says:     Not raised
Gemini says:  granular-checkpointing.md (same lines) AND python-native-foundation.md (line 98)
Assessment:   python-native-foundation.md line 98 reads: "Reserved sheet-evolution storage for
              later character and setting updates". This is a data-field description in a schema
              table, not a claim that sheet-evolution is an active pipeline phase. It accurately
              describes a reserved slot; no update is needed. Gemini's expansion to this file is
              a false positive — the text there is not stale in the same way as the granular-
              checkpointing entries.
Resolution:   M-W-02 scoped to granular-checkpointing.md only, matching Claude's more precise finding.
```

```
[D-04] GPT's broader "backward compatibility" framing vs Claude/Gemini's targeted framing
Claude says:  Fix the test and the docs (two separate findings)
GPT says:     The rename breaks PromptLoader for any direct caller outside ChapterWriterAgent —
              broader compatibility concern; the test is one instance of this
Gemini says:  Fix the test and the docs (same as Claude, separate findings)
Assessment:   GPT's framing is broader and technically accurate — the template rename does affect
              any direct PromptLoader caller. However, the actionable remediation is the same:
              update the test and the docs. GPT merged what Claude and Gemini split into two
              findings (U-C-01 and U-W-01); the substance is equivalent. The "other direct callers"
              concern is addressed by fixing the canonical doc example (U-W-01), which is the
              reference implementation any future caller would follow.
Resolution:   No additional finding needed. U-C-01 and U-W-01 cover the scope.
```
